native_result.HypoB: SES (socioeconomic status). Its effect on BA degree completion falls from a strong positive, highly significant unadjusted logit coefficient (+0.4729, SE 0.0826, p=1.0e-08, OR 1.60) to a small negative, non-robust one (-0.2316, SE 0.1005, p=0.021, OR 0.79; insignificant at alpha=.01, and insignificant at alpha=.05 in sex-stratified and percentile-only variants) once both race and academic characteristics (ASVAB ability composite and class percentile) are included. The apparent SES advantage is channelled almost entirely through measured academic preparation (SES-ABILITY r=.463, SES-PERCENTILE r=.304) and, secondarily, through race (SES-WHITE r=.317): academic characteristics alone absorb 98% of the 0.705 log-odds attenuation, race alone only 17%. Because ABILITY (p=4e-17) and PERCENTILE (p=2e-07) stay strongly predictive while race itself drops to non-significance, controlling for them removes the SES gradient and leaves a near-zero, slightly negative residual direct effect. This is suppression/over-adjustment along the causal pathway from family background to academic preparation to degree attainment, not evidence that higher SES harms BA completion.
